questions.stem: How does variation provide a basis for classifying organisms?

options.text: Patterns of shared and differing traits allow organisms to be grouped
options.why: Members of a group share traits while differing from members of other groups. Classification uses those patterns without claiming that every member is identical.

options.text: Every member of a species has exactly the same observable traits
options.why: Variation occurs within species. Members can differ while still sharing the traits used to place them in the same group.

options.text: Only differences between species are useful for biological classification
options.why: Biologists also study variation within species. Both within-species and between-species patterns matter.

options.text: Each individual must be placed in a separate taxonomic group
options.why: Individual variation doesn't make every organism a separate species. Classification groups organisms using shared characteristics.

questions.stem: Which scientific name is formatted correctly when typed?

options.text: Homo sapiens, with both words italicized
options.why: The genus starts with a capital letter, the specific epithet starts with a lowercase letter, and both words are italicized when typed.

options.text: Homo Sapiens, with both words italicized
options.why: The specific epithet must begin with a lowercase letter. Capitalizing both words breaks the binomial convention.

options.text: homo sapiens, with both words italicized
options.why: The genus must begin with a capital letter. The lowercase specific epithet is the only capitalization used for the second word.

options.text: Homo sapiens, with neither word italicized
options.why: The capitalization is suitable, but typed binomial names require italics. Handwritten names are underlined instead.

questions.stem: Which group meets the biological species concept?

options.text: Organisms that interbreed and produce fertile offspring
options.why: Reproductive compatibility and fertile offspring are the defining evidence in this species concept.

options.text: Organisms that share a habitat and produce any hybrid
options.why: Sharing a habitat doesn't define a species, and a sterile hybrid doesn't meet the fertility requirement.

options.text: Organisms that resemble one another in every visible trait
options.why: That's an overly strict version of morphological classification. Members of one species can show visible variation.

options.text: Organisms that possess the same diploid chromosome number
options.why: Chromosome number is useful evidence, but unrelated species can share a chromosome number. It can't define a species alone.

questions.stem: Why can the boundary between populations and species be unclear during speciation?

options.text: Reproductive isolation usually develops gradually
options.why: Diverging populations change over time, so there may be no single moment when the label must change from population to species.

options.text: Every mutation immediately creates a reproductively isolated species
options.why: One mutation doesn't normally produce a new species. Speciation usually involves accumulated divergence and developing reproductive isolation.

options.text: Geographic separation immediately prevents all future interbreeding
options.why: Separation reduces gene flow, but the populations may remain reproductively compatible for some time. Isolation evolves gradually.

options.text: Morphological differences always appear after reproductive isolation is complete
options.why: Visible differences and reproductive isolation don't follow a fixed order. Either can develop while the populations are diverging.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes a karyogram from a karyotype?

options.text: A karyogram is an arranged chromosome image; a karyotype is the number and appearance of the chromosomes
options.why: The image is the karyogram. The chromosome set described by number, size and other visible features is the karyotype.

options.text: A karyogram is the chromosome number; a karyotype is a complete DNA base sequence
options.why: A karyotype includes chromosome number and appearance, while a karyogram displays the chromosomes. Neither term means a DNA sequence.

options.text: A karyogram contains only sex chromosomes; a karyotype contains only autosomes
options.why: A complete human karyogram displays both autosomes and sex chromosomes. The karyotype also includes both kinds.

options.text: A karyogram records inherited alleles; a karyotype records environmental effects on phenotype
options.why: These terms concern chromosomes, not a separation of genetic and environmental influences. An allele list isn't a karyogram.

questions.stem: Which three features are used to match homologous chromosomes in a karyogram?

options.text: Length, banding pattern and centromere position
options.why: Homologous chromosomes closely match in these three visible features, allowing the images to be paired.

options.text: Gene expression, nucleotide sequence and mutation rate
options.why: Those require molecular or cellular measurements. They aren't the visible features used to arrange a standard karyogram.

options.text: Cell size, nuclear volume and chromosome number
options.why: Those describe the cell or chromosome set. They don't identify which individual chromosomes form a homologous pair.

options.text: DNA mass, allele frequency and protein composition
options.why: Those aren't the three visual criteria available in the chromosome image. Pairing uses chromosome appearance.

questions.stem: Which observation most directly marks the proposed fusion site in human chromosome 2?

options.text: Telomere-like sequences occur in an internal region
options.why: Telomeres normally occur at chromosome ends. Internal telomere-like repeats fit the place where two ancestral ends fused.

options.text: Human cells contain 46 chromosomes rather than 48
options.why: The chromosome count is consistent with fusion, but it doesn't locate the fusion site within chromosome 2.

options.text: Chromosome 2 contains many genes expressed in humans
options.why: A normal chromosome is expected to contain many genes. That observation doesn't distinguish a fused chromosome from any other chromosome.

options.text: Chimpanzees possess a chromosome with the same number label
options.why: Chromosome labels don't establish homology or fusion. Sequence correspondence and unusual internal structures provide the relevant evidence.

options.text: Variation at one nucleotide position within a population
options.why: An SNP is a common form of genomic variation at one base position. Its effect can be neutral or biologically significant.

options.text: Loss of one complete chromosome from a diploid nucleus
options.why: That's a chromosome-number abnormality, not a difference at one nucleotide position.

options.text: Transfer of a plasmid between two bacterial cells
options.why: That's horizontal gene transfer. It moves a DNA molecule rather than defining variation at a single nucleotide.

options.text: A sequence shared without variation by every known organism
options.why: An SNP is defined by variation within a population. A sequence identical in every organism contains no polymorphism at that position.

questions.stem: A lungfish has a much larger genome than a human. Which conclusion is supported?

options.text: The lungfish contains more total DNA
options.why: Genome size measures the amount of DNA. It doesn't reveal complexity or gene number without further evidence.

options.text: The lungfish has more protein-coding genes and greater behavioral complexity
options.why: A larger genome may contain more repetitive or other non-coding DNA. Gene number and behavioral complexity don't follow from total DNA.

options.text: The lungfish belongs to a species with a higher chromosome number
options.why: Genome size and chromosome number are different measurements. A large amount of DNA can be divided among few or many chromosomes.

options.text: The lungfish genome contains no introns or repetitive sequences
options.why: Introns and repetitive sequences contribute to eukaryotic genome size. Their absence can't be inferred and would work against this explanation.

questions.stem: Which use of whole genome sequencing is part of personalized medicine?

options.text: Choosing treatment using a patient’s genetic variants
options.why: Genomic variants can help predict treatment response or disease risk, allowing care to be tailored to the patient.

options.text: Arranging stained chromosomes into homologous pairs by length
options.why: That's construction of a karyogram. It uses chromosome images rather than the complete nucleotide sequence.

options.text: Naming a species from its visible structural characteristics
options.why: That's use of the morphological species concept. Whole genome sequencing compares DNA across the entire genome.

options.text: Measuring environmental effects without collecting genetic information
options.why: Personalized genomics depends on genetic information. A method that excludes it can't be an application of genome sequencing.

questions.stem: Why does horizontal gene transfer make bacterial species difficult to define?

options.text: DNA can move between separate evolutionary lineages
options.why: A bacterium can acquire genes from a non-parent, sometimes from another species. Its genome may therefore combine DNA from different lineages.

options.text: Every transferred gene prevents bacteria from reproducing asexually
options.why: Bacteria can continue reproducing after acquiring DNA. The classification problem comes from genes crossing lineage boundaries.

options.text: Transferred DNA always changes the bacterial chromosome number
options.why: Horizontal transfer concerns movement of DNA sequences. It doesn't have to alter the number of chromosomes.

options.text: Bacteria produce sterile hybrids after transferring plasmids
options.why: Plasmid transfer isn't mating and doesn't produce hybrid offspring. Fertility language from sexual reproduction doesn't fit this process.

options.text: Their chromosomes can’t all form homologous pairs during meiosis
options.why: A mule has 63 chromosomes inherited from parents with different chromosome numbers. Irregular pairing makes balanced gamete production unlikely.

options.text: Their body cells contain no homologous chromosomes at all
options.why: Many mule chromosomes do have related partners. The problem is that the full set can't pair and separate normally.

options.text: Their chromosomes fail to replicate before every mitotic division
options.why: Mules grow through ordinary mitosis, which requires chromosome replication. Their fertility problem appears during meiosis.

options.text: Their parents contribute identical haploid chromosome sets
options.why: Horse and donkey chromosome sets differ. If the sets were identical and paired normally, this source of sterility wouldn't occur.

questions.stem: Which pair of statements is suitable for one step of a dichotomous key?

options.text: Leaves opposite on stem / leaves alternate on stem
options.why: The statements are observable, contrasting alternatives about the same feature. Each specimen can be directed along one route.

options.text: Flowers attractive / flowers less attractive than average
options.why: Attractiveness is subjective and the alternatives aren't defined consistently. A key needs observable, unambiguous traits.

options.text: Animal is small / animal has six legs and two antennae
options.why: The statements compare different features and aren't mutually exclusive. A small animal could also have six legs and two antennae.

options.text: Species evolved recently / species evolved in a different habitat
options.why: Those claims usually can't be observed from the specimen, and both could be true. They won't produce a reliable identification route.

questions.stem: What can a close DNA-barcode match from a lake-water sample establish?

options.text: The matched species contributed DNA to the sample
options.why: The sequence match provides evidence that DNA from that species was present in the sampled water.

options.text: A known number of living individuals occupied the lake
options.why: Environmental DNA can come from dead material and shedding rates vary. A match doesn't provide a dependable count of living individuals.

options.text: The matched species currently reproduces throughout the entire lake
options.why: One water sample records DNA at its sampling place and time. It doesn't demonstrate reproduction or distribution across the whole lake.

options.text: The complete genome of every organism in the lake was sequenced
options.why: DNA barcoding targets short identification regions. It isn't whole genome sequencing of every organism present.
